units.translation: ⟦1⟧ Dindorf restored here and at ⟦2⟧ for -⟦3⟧, cf. Kühner-Blass II, 460; on ⟦4⟧ (Porson) at ⟦5⟧. Paley compares Homeric ⟦6⟧ (⟦7⟧ 242). Third episode, part 1: 566 - (777)915. The following trial scene I can only imagine on the Areopagus, which is also named at line (688.) 693; so during the preceding stasimon a small scene change was again carried out. On the Areopagus there was no building, and all proceedings of the blood courts took place under the open sky (Antiphon 5, 11, Aristotle ⟦8⟧. ⟦9⟧. 57, 4), to avoid pollution by remaining in the same space; accordingly the scene is to be imagined here as well. Thus the backdrop of a temple building, which was present at the beginning and also later, had to be concealed now, just as for the first part of the Choephori (Ch. Introduction p. 20); but the ekkyklema, which last displayed the interior of the temple with the image of the goddess, could remain, and it was only necessary to draw the image back again and instead to set up seating for the Areopagites. These were, as the scholiast notes, a mute parachoregema; how many there were is not said, and indeed this council had no fixed number of members; twelve, however, as many as the chorus comprised, were fully sufficient, and this number has also been inferred from 711 ff., see below. The people, however, the corona, is present only in imagination (⟦10⟧ 566); but a herald had to actually appear, and a trumpeter. These appear, like the Areopagites, in the retinue of Athena, and likewise, I think, her suppliant Orestes. The trial is only in a free manner an image or model of those taking place before the Areopagus. Athena presides and directs, which in reality the ⟦11⟧ did; naturally the accuser has the first word, but of the double procedure with ⟦12⟧ and ⟦13⟧ for each party (⟦14⟧) there is nothing here, rather the speeches are dramatically dissolved into dialogue between the parties. That no diomosia of the parties takes place, which existed before the Areopagus, and indeed in the most solemn manner (Dem. 23, 67 ff.), has already been pointed out (p. 122). According to the later arrangement, here, where the accused admits the deed but asserts its justice, the Areopagus would not have been competent at all, but the court at the Delphinion (Dem. 23, 74 ff.); but rightly and in accordance with tradition Aeschylus has only this one blood court, competent for all cases, founded first. The secret voting with pebbles in urns, as described here, certainly existed also in these courts, as in the ordinary ones.
